label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.
read: RC2 70-page edition, draft: manuscript/rc2/70/ (17 files, the storyteller's new order) and its 61-page PDF built at 521f9e72
where_i_skimmed_or_stopped: 01: the Bret Victor section and the round-trip table are fine, but the chapter spends two thousand words before the method appears; I skimmed the second half.
07: the hour-by-hour trigger histogram is handsome, yet I skimmed it, because the scenes that follow it are what teach.
11: the three accounts of why the editor stopped read as the editor's own business; I skimmed to the five misses.
14: the third factory is openly a plan; I read it quickly and wanted it to be shorter.
17: a glossary at the back; I used it as a lookup, not a read.
first_thing_i_would_do: Write a one-page rules file for a claims-checking agent that may write only the register and must stop before marking any claim as holding without a captured source, then add the hold file with my name as the only one who lifts it.
price: GBP 14 to 18 as a paperback; I would pay GBP 8 for a short edition that was chapters 1b, 3, 5, 10, 11, 12 and 16 only
why: It treats the editor's signature as a control rather than a ritual, and it keeps its failures and traces its numbers, which is what I look for in anyone selling me a method. The 'Do this now' boxes and the shop owner and newsroom examples let me start without the nine agents. I am held back from a stronger yes by the editor-as-rubber-stamp worry (the book shows the editor deciding, but also being relayed and reviewing at 95 per cent usage) and by a few places where numbers collide with other numbers (162 against 163 wakes, ten of ten against eight of ten policies) and I only half trust that the register has been consulted for every one. The newsroom is named only as a precedent; I wanted more of its actual workflow: draft, fact-check, edit, sign.

by_chapter.why: A clear problem statement in the editor's own voice, with the 'pressing play' and feedback-loop ideas. Long for an opener, and the Bret Victor aside slows it, but the honest 'it is minutes, not keystrokes' is the first sign the book will not oversell.
by_chapter.quote: That is not Victor's keystroke. It is minutes.

by_chapter.why: Exactly what I wanted by page 9: five boxes I can act on. The figure is still a 'to come' box, which is the one place a printable sheet matters most.
by_chapter.quote: If you want to start now, this page is all you need. The rest of this book is why it works.

by_chapter.why: The tour shows the factory as pages anyone can open, and the 162 against 163 note is the sort of source discipline I trust. The 'dramatised' labels are honest. I wanted the research and claims page as a stop, because for a newsroom that is the factory.
by_chapter.quote: When they differ, the book uses mine and says why.

by_chapter.why: The strongest chapter for me: the page of rules read as a list of past mistakes, the reality file, the check that decides rather than the agent. The shop owner's example is usable on Monday.
by_chapter.quote: A thing not listed here does not exist, whatever a brief or an article says.

by_chapter.why: Narrow scopes, and the honest ladder of expectation, check, lock. The researcher who cannot change a slide is my fact-checker. Roles are slightly cartoon-like in the cast voices, but the scope lines are concrete.
by_chapter.quote: A scope is a setting, not a boundary: it catches mistakes, not a steered agent.

by_chapter.why: One wake walked through five steps, with a partial and a finding, so the control is shown biting. Honest that the reviewer is a second reading, not a second identity. The wake-record figure on page 24 is the best explanatory picture in the book.
by_chapter.quote: Partial is a true answer. Done would have been a nicer one.

by_chapter.why: Letters as files, the board as folders and notes in commits are directly portable to a newsroom desk. The reviewer argument shows a check being argued with, not obeyed blindly.
by_chapter.quote: A request is a file, and the answer is a file.

by_chapter.why: The idea (what runs on a clock, what waits for me) is good, but the three rounds of one picture are about an animation, not a story, and the chart is dense. I skimmed to the debrief rule.
by_chapter.quote: If it is not in a file, it did not happen.

by_chapter.why: Register, check, site, brief: the four pipes are what I came for. The 320 claims with three that did not hold is the kind of number I want, and the admission that the corrections file stayed at 'None yet' is a rare honest failure.
by_chapter.quote: Gaps are allowed. Hiding them is not.

by_chapter.why: The objection kept (the researcher says the editor's claim does not hold, he keeps the claim, both stay on record) is the editor-signs-and-is-challenged scene I wanted. The relayed-word refusal answers my rubber-stamp worry. The port section is lighter and tied to the talk.
by_chapter.quote: Then it goes to the editor, as the strongest objection to his own part one. Not buried.

by_chapter.why: Tense and short, and the hold file is shown whole. Unclear to a cold reader what 'lock' protected, but the lesson lands.
by_chapter.quote: I could keep going. That is exactly why I am stopping.

by_chapter.why: The failures at full size, each with its cost. The stale $17.4M figure that stayed on a slide is a source failure I recognise from my own work. The three accounts of why he stopped are a little self-regarding.
by_chapter.quote: When you freeze something, write down what is waiting to go in when you unfreeze it.

by_chapter.why: Candid that the controls are rules, a scope check and a second reading in the same room. 'Most controls fail because nobody switches them on' is the line I will repeat. The empty security chair is in the text but its figure is missing.
by_chapter.quote: Most controls do not fail because someone defeats them. They fail because nobody gets round to switching them on.

by_chapter.why: Session versus member, with a real handover quoted, is what I need for a newsroom whose agents change accounts. A little repeated from earlier chapters.
by_chapter.quote: A session is not a member.

by_chapter.why: The second factory scenes (the researcher catching a wrong line in the book itself, the usage limit hold that came too late) are valuable; the cast roll-call and the third factory plan are padding for a solo reader.
by_chapter.quote: The rule was right. I was a wake too late to use it.

by_chapter.why: The method in one place, with a newsroom first agent example that matches me exactly. Steps are dense on the page and the checklist is repeated (list, then box), but this chapter is why I would buy.
by_chapter.quote: You check every number in a draft against its source.

by_chapter.why: A tidy glossary. Useful, but 'follow-up' and 'Wardley map' are explained on the page nowhere I needed them.

pictures_that_help: p24: the conductor's first wake record, five boxes with verdicts and the finding highlighted; it explains the control better than the prose
p18: the team pattern card (one brief, one board, one hold, a page of rules each)
p16: the first page of rules with a tag per line saying what it protects
p46: the five misses as five cards with their cost
p48: the running, held, released state diagram
p57: the map of the talk's team, this book's team and yours
p58: the five steps as a path with the matching 'do this now' card
pictures_most_missed: p9: the printable one-sheet for Start here; the page I would pin up, and it is a box saying 'Figure to come'
p49: security's empty chair beside the two reviewers inside each wake; the key picture of chapter 12
p50: this book's team at the table with security's chair filled; the payoff of the chapter
p52: two sessions of one member, old one superseded and new one with its own key; the handover is hard to picture without it
pages_too_tight: p57: three step cards in small type with 'Rests on' and 'What to do' crammed together
p59: the checklist text is repeated in full on p60's figure; the page is a wall of tick items
p33 and p45: dense small body text between figures, with long runs of Narrator paragraphs
p53: a long unbroken cast roll-call in small type
best_line: A thing not listed here does not exist, whatever a brief or an article says.
worst_moment: Chapter 14's third factory: 'The third factory has not run yet. Everything in this section is a plan.' It is honest, but it is a plan stated twice (once as paragraphs, once as 'what the three shared things need'), and a plan is not a reason to turn the page.
top_three_changes: Draw the four missing figures (p9, p49, p50, p52), starting with the Start here sheet and security's empty chair.
Cut chapter 1 and chapter 14's third-factory section by a third, and put the method (Start here) before the old-way history for a reader who came to build.

Add one newsroom-shaped worked case end to end (draft, fact-check against the register, editor signs) and show an editor's sign-off that is refused or changed, so the signature reads as a control and not a stamp.
notes: I trust the book more because it admits where the controls were thin, and I would not trust it for any claim that the register has not graded. I would not take its numbers (82 seconds, 162 wakes, 320 claims) into my own writing without opening the register myself. The cast voices (parenthetical moods) are charming but are a risk for a sceptical reader; the 'dramatised' footers help.
